title: Adam, told again
hookLine: the steward, the names, the bowing, the return (2:30–38)
last: NOTHING IS TOO SMALL TO TEACH.

lines: THE BOOK YOU LOVED AT TWELVE.
cards: Reread a book you loved at twelve, and something odd happens. The plot is the same; you know how it ends.
But you notice things you walked straight past: a sentence on page three that sets up everything, a character you'd ignored. The story didn't change. The reader did, and so did where it's read from.
On day twenty-two of this path, you met Adam. Now he comes back, in his place inside al-Baqarah. Today: Adam.

teach.b: Last year you met the story in pieces. The steward: “Lo! I am about to place a viceroy in the earth.” The names Adam was taught and the angels weren't.
The bowing, and Iblis who refused. The slip in the garden, and the words of return. This year, read it where it sits.

Just before it, al-Baqarah has described three kinds of people, mindful, refusing, and in between, and asked how anyone can turn from God who gave them life. Then, without a break, it goes back to the very beginning.
Some readers hear it as: here is where all three kinds of people come from. Look at the angels.

teach.h: A QUESTION IS NOT A REFUSAL
teach.b: When God announces a steward, they ask an honest question: will You place there one who will spread corruption and shed blood, while we praise You? It isn't defiance, and it gets an answer: I know what you do not know.
The one who refuses isn't the one who asked. It's Iblis, who here simply refuses, and is proud; in another surah he gives his reason: I am better than him. And look at the ending.

teach.h: IT ENDS WITH A PROMISE OF GUIDANCE
teach.b: Adam and his wife are sent down, and God says guidance will come to them from Him, and whoever follows it will have no fear and will not grieve.
Guidance: the word the Fatiha asked for, and the word al-Baqarah used for itself in verse two. The Qur'an tells Adam's story in several surahs, each from a different angle.

how: Muslims meet Adam's story in several surahs, including al-Baqarah, al-A'raf and Ta-Ha, and teachers often read each telling for what it adds, rather than treating them as repeats.

o: the first prophet to be given a written book of law
an angel who questioned God and was sent out of the garden
the steward, taught the names, who slipped and turned back

games.q: Adam, told again — tap the pairs.

s: the angels in the story refuse to bow
they ask a question and are answered; it's Iblis who refuses.
al-Baqarah's telling of Adam ends with a promise of guidance
whoever follows it will have no fear and will not grieve.
the Qur'an tells Adam's story only once
it returns in several surahs, each from a different angle.

games.q: you're one of the angels. God announces a steward on earth, one who could shed blood. what do you do?
games.why: the angels ask: will You place there one who will spread corruption? and God answers: I know what you do not know. asking isn't refusing.

practice: Let the story from day twenty-two come back in your own order, without checking: the angels, the names, the bowing, Iblis turning away, the garden and the tree, the words Adam received.
Notice which part is clearest, which you'd forgotten, and what you see now that you didn't last year.

wordCard.voice: Adam. The steward, taught the names, who slipped and turned back. In al-Baqarah his story ends with a promise of guidance. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: guidance; the word that links the Fatiha, al-Baqarah's second verse, and the end of Adam's story.

carryVoice: Your line: the story comes back deeper. Each telling of Adam adds something new. See you tomorrow.
